title: It starts with a question people are almost afraid to say out loud:
paragraphs: It starts with a question people are almost afraid to say out loud:
“If Cain married his sister… wasn’t that sin?”
Pause.

Because this isn’t just about biology.
This is about how sin began—and how grace responds.
First, the text.
In Genesis 4:17, it simply says:
“Cain knew his wife…”
But it never names her.
Why?
Because earlier, in Genesis 5:4, we’re told that Adam and Eve had “other sons and daughters.”
Meaning—yes.
Cain’s wife was most likely his sister or close relative.
Now here’s the tension.
Isn’t that incest? Isn’t that sinful?
Today—yes. Clearly.
God later forbids it in laws like Leviticus 18.
But here’s what we miss…

Sin is not defined by human discomfort.
Sin is defined by God’s command.
And at the beginning—those commands were different.

Early humanity was genetically pure, untouched by generations of corruption.
There was no law yet prohibiting close-family marriage.
So at that moment in history:

It was necessary.
It was permitted.
It was not yet called sin.
Some scholars interpret this as a temporary allowance for the survival of humanity until population expanded and moral law was more fully revealed.
But don’t miss the deeper story.

We get stuck asking, “Who did Cain marry?”
When the real question is:
“What did Cain become?”

A murderer.
A wanderer.
A marked man running from God.
And yet…
God didn’t destroy him.
God protected him.
In Genesis 4:15, God places a mark—not of shame alone—but of mercy.
Let that hit.
The first killer received protection from God.
And that’s where grace walks in.

Because the Bible is not a clean family tree.
It’s a broken bloodline that God refuses to abandon.

From Cain’s generation of sin…
to a Savior born generations later.
Enter Jesus.

Where Cain took life,
Christ gave His.

Where Cain hid,
Jesus was exposed on the cross.

Where Cain was marked for protection,
Jesus was wounded for redemption.
So yes—early human relationships were different.
But the bigger truth?

Sin entered the world through one family…
and salvation came through another.
There’s a reason you’re asking these questions.

God isn’t afraid of your doubts.
He answers them with truth—and then offers you grace.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
